target.title: fix(openrouter): add model-aware tool schema normalization for proxied providers
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Models routed through OpenRouter that reject `anyOf`/`oneOf` in tool parameter schemas (Moonshot/Kimi K3, DeepSeek, Google/Gemini) receive raw unsanitized schemas and return HTTP 400 — "provider rejected the request schema or tool payload."

The ClawRouter extension already handles this via `resolveToolFamily()` model-prefix routing, but the OpenRouter extension registers no `normalizeToolSchemas` or `inspectToolSchemas` hooks. Tool schemas pass through verbatim regardless of the downstream provider.

## Why This Change Was Made

Kimi K3 (`moonshotai/kimi-k3`) via OpenRouter fails on tool calls that include `anyOf`/`oneOf` unions in parameter schemas — common in MCP-sourced tools and TypeBox-defined tools. The model handles basic chat completions fine, but 400s on tool payloads.

The root cause: `extensions/openrouter/index.ts` has no tool schema normalization, unlike `extensions/clawrouter/index.ts` which routes models to the correct compat family (`deepseek`, `gemini`, `openai`) based on model ID prefix.

## User Impact

Users running Moonshot/Kimi, DeepSeek, or Google models through OpenRouter will no longer get `400 Provider returned error` on tool calls. The fix applies the same schema normalization that direct provider plugins and ClawRouter already use.

## Evidence

- Observed in production: `moonshotai/kimi-k3` via OpenRouter returns 200 for basic chat but 400 when tools with `anyOf`/`oneOf` schemas are included
- `providerRuntimeFailureKind: "schema"` in gateway diagnostic logs
- ClawRouter already implements the identical pattern at `extensions/clawrouter/index.ts:105-117`
- DeepSeek direct provider uses `buildProviderToolCompatFamilyHooks("deepseek")` at `extensions/deepseek/index.ts:55`
- 7 tests covering Moonshot/Kimi, OpenAI passthrough, Google, and DeepSeek model routing — including 3 regression tests for canonical `openrouter/`-prefixed model IDs
- All OpenRouter extension tests pass

### Live behavior proof

Gateway running this PR's dev build (OpenClaw 2026.7.1, commit 21d58559). Model: `openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k3` — canonical OpenRouter-prefixed ID, the exact case the second commit addresses.

| 10 | read | string + optional ints | ✅ 200 |

The `cron` and `image_generate` calls are the critical ones — their schemas carry `anyOf` unions and nested object definitions, exactly what Moonshot rejects un-normalized. Both went through clean on the patched build. 10/10 tool calls succeeded; zero 400s.

target.title: Manage Claw MCP server ownership
target.body:
## Summary

- apply portable stdio and remote MCP declarations through OpenClaw's validated source-config writer
- preserve `${ENV_VAR}` references and credential-free OAuth intent without storing server configuration in provenance
- classify each declaration with the shared Claw ownership model: `relationship` (`managed` or `referenced`), `origin` (`claw-introduced` or `pre-existing`), and current `independentOwner` evidence
- expose MCP ownership and drift in status/export, reconcile uncertain writes, and support the same explicit referenced-cleanup choices as skills and plugins

## Contract

- dry-run shows each MCP command or URL before consent; apply rechecks source config and uses create-only writes
- a collision-free declaration created for the first Claw is managed; an exact pre-existing declaration, or reuse by another Claw, is referenced
- conflicting existing names block add; exact declarations are reused without mutation
- ordinary MCP configuration writes mark current independent ownership; Claw writes do not claim an independent owner
- provenance stores only agent, name, config digest, relationship, origin, current independent-owner evidence, and lifecycle status
- pending writes reconcile deterministically against source-preserving config for both landed and non-landed outcomes
- remove deletes unchanged managed declarations by default; referenced declarations are retained unless the integrity-bound plan selects `remove-if-unused` or an explicit `mcp:<name>` cleanup, with conflict override required when another owner remains
- compare-before-unset prevents removing a declaration that changed after planning; unreadable source config fails closed
- ordinary OpenClaw MCP and agent lifecycles remain authoritative and unchanged

## Verification

- generated Kysely schema verification: passed
- Kysely raw-SQL guardrails: passed
- scoped Oxfmt, Oxlint, and `git diff --check`: passed
- 126 focused schema, MCP, config, lifecycle, export, CLI, and ordinary agent-delete tests passed on exact head `1d9aca04a38`
- live MCP process startup was not exercised; this PR mutates and verifies source configuration only

```text
Test Files  7 passed (7)
Tests       126 passed (126)
```

## Stack

- RFC: https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/27
- Depends on: #102383 Gateway cron ownership
- This PR: validated MCP source config, common ownership semantics, reconciliation, export, and safe removal
- Next: #102427 projects the complete lifecycle state into doctor diagnostics

MCP remains a separate stage because OpenClaw config, rather than the agent entry or Gateway scheduler, owns these declarations. The experimental CLI remains gated by `OPENCLAW_EXPERIMENTAL_CLAWS=1`.

target.title: Manage Claw cron jobs through the gateway
target.body:
## Summary

- install grouped Claw cron declarations through the gateway-owned `cron.add` API
- persist pending, complete, failed, or removed ownership references keyed by final agent id and declaration id
- expose cron ownership in status, round-trip complete declarations through export, and include exact cron state in remove consent
- disable Claw-owned recurring work before agent config, package, or workspace cleanup
- compose existing OpenClaw config, session, workspace-safety, and trash primitives without changing ordinary agent deletion behavior

## Contract

- scheduler mutation stays in the gateway; Claws never write the cron store directly
- declaration keys are scoped as `claw:<agent-id>:<manifest-job-id>`, so package-local ids do not collide globally
- response-lost retries reconcile by declaration key before issuing another `cron.add`
- `main` declarations target `session:agent:<final-agent-id>:main`; `isolated` remains isolated, and strict v1 validation rejects other session modes
- removal calls `cron.remove` before any agent/config mutation and records partial state if recurring work cannot be proven disabled
- Claw removal uses provenance-aware cleanup around shared lower-level OpenClaw primitives; the normal `agents delete` command and gateway behavior are unchanged
- the durable install record retains its last completed phase (`config_committed`) when cron installation fails, while the command result is `partial` and includes failed cron provenance for retry/doctor

## Stack

- RFC: https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/27
- Depends on: #102306 grouped export
- This PR: gateway-owned cron mutation, provenance, status, export, and removal
- Next: #102406 validated MCP ownership

All behavior remains gated by `OPENCLAW_EXPERIMENTAL_CLAWS=1`.

## Validation

- 59 focused cron, provenance, lifecycle, and ordinary agent-delete tests passed on exact head `344d024f8b5`
- scoped Oxfmt, Oxlint, and `git diff --check`: passed
- emitted `cron.add` payload is validated by the gateway protocol validator
- fresh GitHub CI is running after correcting the stale type/test fixtures found by the preceding run

## Real behavior proof

The lifecycle tests prove consent-bound add, scheduler-id provenance, response-lost reconciliation, status/export visibility, and removal ordering. A scheduler failure returns partial with `agentRemoved: false`; successful removal disables Claw-owned recurring work before the provenance-aware local lifecycle proceeds.

target.title: fix(synology-chat): stop fabricating send message ids
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Synology Chat outbound sends fabricated a platform message id. After the incoming-webhook `sendMessage`/`sendFileUrl` calls resolve with a bare `true` (`extensions/synology-chat/src/client.ts:96`, `:132` — `Promise<boolean>`, no id in the webhook contract), the adapter returned `messageId: \`sc-${Date.now()}\`` and stamped that synthetic id into the delivery receipt's `primaryPlatformMessageId`, `platformMessageIds`, and `parts` (`extensions/synology-chat/src/channel.ts`). Downstream consumers treat `messageId` as a real platform id (e.g. delivery-pin lookup in `src/infra/outbound/deliver.ts`), so a fabricated id can be acted on as if it were deliverable platform state. This is the same shape as the merged nostr fix #110006, which removed the synthetic `nostr-${Date.now()}` id in favor of an honest send result.

## Why This Change Was Made

The plugin-sdk contract already defines the sanctioned representation for "no platform id": the empty string sentinel. `createEmptyChannelResult` documents that "empty message ids are the legacy 'no platform id' sentinel expected by outbound callers" (`src/plugin-sdk/channel-send-result.ts:55`), and `buildChannelSendResult` normalizes a missing id to `""` (`src/plugin-sdk/channel-send-result.ts:120`). Sibling channels that receive no platform id from their transport (qqbot `extensions/qqbot/src/channel.ts:52`, googlechat `extensions/googlechat/src/channel.adapters.ts:52`) pass an empty `results` array to `createMessageReceiptFromOutboundResults`, producing a receipt with no platform ids and no parts. This change adopts exactly that shape: `messageId: ""` and a receipt built from an empty results array (keeping `threadId` = chat id for routing context only). Note the receipt builder falls back from `messageId` to `chatId` when resolving a part id (`src/channels/message/receipt.ts:17-27`), so passing the chat id alongside an empty message id would have re-laundered the chat id into a fake platform message id; the empty-results form avoids that. Downstream is safe for the sentinel: the delivery-pin path explicitly guards `if (!params.messageId)` (`src/infra/outbound/deliver.ts:1075`), and result aggregation uses truthiness (`deliver.ts:2572`, `:2618`). Scope is limited to the two send paths; no SDK or core changes.

## User Impact

Successful Synology Chat text and media sends now report an empty message id and a receipt with no platform message ids instead of a plausible-looking but fake `sc-<timestamp>` id. Delivery itself is unchanged; only the reported send metadata becomes honest. Operators relying on delivery receipts will no longer see synthetic ids that cannot be resolved on the NAS.

## Evidence

- Precedent: #110006 (merged) removed the identical `nostr-${Date.now()}` fabrication in the nostr adapter.
- Tests: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/synology-chat` — with the fix, `channel.test.ts` is 40 passed / 41 total, and the full plugin suite shows 120 passed with 3 failures that reproduce identically on unmodified `origin/main` (`5143d909b9`): two setup-wizard prompt failures in `core.test.ts` and `setup status honors the selected named account` in `channel.test.ts` (locale-dependent wizard prompt expectations, unrelated to this change).
- Reverse verification: with only `channel.ts` stashed, the three updated/new assertions fail (`declares message adapter durable text and media with receipt proofs`, `sendText returns an honest empty-id result on success`, `sendMedia returns an honest empty-id result on success`); with the fix restored, all three pass.
- New/updated coverage: `sendText`/`sendMedia` success tests now assert `messageId === ""`, `receipt.primaryPlatformMessageId === undefined`, empty `platformMessageIds`/`parts`, and `receipt.threadId === chatId`; the message-adapter capability proof test asserts the same honest receipt shape for both text and media.
- Typecheck: `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.extensions.json` — zero errors in touched code; only the 3 pre-existing `packages/net-policy/src/ip.ts` errors that also occur on clean `origin/main`.
- `git diff --check` clean; `oxfmt --check` clean on both touched files.
- Diff stat: 2 files, +43/-20 (prod `channel.ts` net −6 lines).

target.title: fix(scripts): bound release CI summary GitHub lookups
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The release CI summary helper performs multiple sequential `gh` API reads during full release validation. Each read used `execFileSync` without a timeout, so one stalled GitHub request could block the surrounding workflow job until the 120-minute budget expires.

## Why This Change Was Made

The default `gh` runner now routes through a caller-owned `execFileSync` with a 60-second timeout and `SIGKILL`, and applies the same bound to artifact zip downloads. This keeps the release-specific latency budget local, preserves the existing 64 MiB output allowance, covers all lookups (REST reads and artifact zip downloads), and continues to fail closed when a lookup cannot complete.

The runner accepts an `execFileSyncImpl` injection point and an optional `timeoutMs` parameter, allowing the exact production options and error propagation to be tested without a slow timer-based test.

## User Impact

A release CI summary lookup no longer waits indefinitely on a stalled GitHub request. Healthy validation behavior is unchanged; a lookup that exceeds one minute now fails clearly so the release can be diagnosed or retried.

## Evidence

Exact head: \`${HEAD_SHA}\`, based on `593423ecc0d3c1d883e247a6fca568e312791eec`.

- Focused test: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run test/scripts/release-ci-summary.test.ts` - 45/45 passed (including 4 `runReleaseCiGh` tests).

target.title: fix(agents): avoid symlink-follow in auth.json bootstrap
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a local attacker with write access to the `auth.json` parent directory can redirect credential-store bootstrap writes through a symlink. `AuthStorage` is the default credential backend for agent sessions, and its bootstrap path creates `auth.json` when the file is missing. On current `main`, a planted dangling `auth.json` symlink causes bootstrap to create, truncate, and chmod the symlink target outside the auth directory.

This also closes the follow-up hardening gap ClawSweeper found in the atomic replacement wrapper: after `@openclaw/fs-safe` renames the temp file into place, it performs a best-effort final `chmod` by target path. An attacker who can write the parent directory can swap `auth.json` back to a symlink in that post-rename window and redirect the chmod to another path.

## Why This Change Was Made

Root cause is in `src/agents/sessions/auth-storage.ts`, `FileAuthStorageBackend.ensureFileExists()`:

```ts
private ensureFileExists(): void {
  if (!existsSync(this.authPath)) {
    writeFileSync(this.authPath, "{}", "utf-8");
    chmodSync(this.authPath, 0o600);
  }
}
```

`existsSync`, `writeFileSync`, and `chmodSync` all operate on the final path. When `auth.json` is a symlink to a missing target, the check sees no existing target and the create/chmod operations land on the symlink target.

The existing persist path already uses `replaceAuthFileAtomic()`, which writes a sibling temp file with the requested file mode and renames it into place. This PR routes bootstrap through that path:

```ts
private ensureFileExists(): void {
  if (!existsSync(this.authPath)) {
    this.replaceAuthFileAtomic("{}");
  }
}
```

To close the active swap gap, `src/infra/replace-file.ts` now wraps both async and sync `replaceFileAtomic` calls so OpenClaw sets the temp file to the requested or preserved mode before rename through a no-follow file descriptor, then skips the redundant final chmod of the replacement path. The wrapper keeps parent-directory chmod behavior and exact final file modes while removing the post-rename target-path chmod that can follow a swapped symlink. If fs-safe takes its copy fallback, the wrapper restores the resolved mode on the opened destination descriptor instead of chmodding the final path. The async wrapper resolves preserveExistingMode lazily inside the serialized replacement phase, so same-path queued writes preserve the mode left by the earlier replacement instead of an old pre-queue stat.

## User Impact

Operators no longer expose an arbitrary-file create/truncate/chmod primitive through the credential store when `auth.json` is absent and its parent directory is writable by another local user. Normal behavior is unchanged: missing `auth.json` is still created as a real `{}` file at mode `0o600`.

## Evidence

Local verification:

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/infra/replace-file.test.ts src/infra/json-files.test.ts`: 2 files passed, 24 assertions passed.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/sessions/auth-storage.symlink-bootstrap.test.ts src/agents/sessions/auth-storage.test.ts`: 2 files passed, 3 assertions passed.
- `./node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check src/infra/replace-file.ts src/infra/replace-file.test.ts src/agents/sessions/auth-storage.ts src/agents/sessions/auth-storage.symlink-bootstrap.test.ts`: clean.
- `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs src/infra/replace-file.ts src/infra/replace-file.test.ts src/agents/sessions/auth-storage.ts src/agents/sessions/auth-storage.symlink-bootstrap.test.ts`: clean.
- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.core.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/core.tsbuildinfo`: clean.
- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.core.test.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/core-test.tsbuildinfo`: clean.
- Added a same-path async preserveExistingMode regression that queues a 0644 replacement ahead of a preserveExistingMode replacement and verifies the queued write keeps 0644.

## Real behavior proof
Behavior addressed: `AuthStorage` bootstrap no longer writes through a planted `auth.json` symlink, and OpenClaw's atomic replacement wrapper no longer chmods a symlink target swapped into place after rename while still preserving exact requested modes on rename, copy fallback, and queued same-path replacements.
Real environment tested: the real `AuthStorage` class from `src/agents/sessions/auth-storage.ts` and the real `replaceFileAtomicSync` and `replaceFileAtomic` wrappers from `src/infra/replace-file.ts` were driven against real on-disk temp directories on pristine `origin/main` afe00f6c7b72f4d21f5b48b42b6792507ed7cd7d and PR head 1d2a83a50ae80f2e48654b6122eada5341c402cb. The static symlink and queued same-path scenarios used normal filesystem calls. The post-rename swap and fallback scenarios used an instrumented filesystem object only to force the relevant filesystem outcome at the production helper boundary.
Exact steps or command run after this patch: `PATH=/opt/node/bin:$PATH node --import tsx /tmp/openclaw-bug-repros/102853/proof-driver.ts` from `/root/openclaw`, first with `src/agents/sessions/auth-storage.ts` and `src/infra/replace-file.ts` reset to pristine `origin/main`, then with the same files restored from PR head 1d2a83a50ae80f2e48654b6122eada5341c402cb.
Evidence after fix:

target.title: fix(admin-http-rpc): reject oversized declared request bodies
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Admin HTTP RPC callers could declare a JSON request body larger than the 1 MiB route limit using a valid decimal `Content-Length` outside JavaScript's safe-integer range, leaving the request to wait for a body instead of returning the structured 413 response.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Admin HTTP RPC handler compares decimal `Content-Length` digits directly with the route limit before reading the body. This preserves precision for arbitrarily large valid declarations while retaining the existing streamed-overflow response and cleanup path.

## User Impact

Operators and host tooling using `POST /api/v1/admin/rpc` now receive the same HTTP 413 JSON response for every valid oversized declared length, including values beyond JavaScript's safe integer range. The rejected request does not reach Gateway RPC dispatch.

target.title: fix(ui): workboard dropdowns could clip in short windows
target.body:
Related: #110621

## What Problem This Solves

Follow-up to #110621's review finding, applied to the sibling surface: the workboard select dropdowns capped their listbox height with a viewport-only bound (`min(320px, calc(100vh - 48px))`, `260px` on narrow screens), overriding Web Awesome's collision-aware `--auto-size-available-height`. When the popup opens with little room on either side of the control — short windows, toolbars near the bottom edge — a long status/agent list could overflow or clip instead of shrinking and scrolling.

## Why This Change Was Made

Same composition proven in #110621: keep the design cap but bound it by Web Awesome's computed available height, `min(<cap>, var(--auto-size-available-height, calc(100vh - 48px)))`, in both the desktop and narrow-viewport rules. The viewport fallback only applies if the variable is ever unset.

## User Impact

Workboard dropdowns (status, agent pickers) now always fit the space the popup actually has, scrolling internally instead of clipping in constrained layouts.

## Evidence

`oxfmt --check ui/src/styles/workboard.css` clean. The identical composition was verified empirically on the settings language picker in #110621: in a 420px-tall viewport the listbox's resolved max-height followed `--auto-size-available-height` (216px), stayed fully on-screen, and scrolled internally. Both workboard cap sites (desktop 320px, ≤640px 260px) get the same treatment; CSS-only diff (+4/−2).

target.title: fix(qqbot): bound remote media downloads with header and idle timeouts
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

QQBot remote-media downloads could hang indefinitely when an upstream CDN
accepted the connection, returned headers (and optionally one body chunk), then
stopped sending data. Two channel-owned callers were missing a body-idle bound:

- `getPlatformAdapter().downloadFile` called `readRemoteMediaBuffer` with no
  header/idle timeouts
- `file-utils.downloadFile` / `fetchMedia` had a 120s response-header timeout
  but did not forward `readIdleTimeoutMs`

## Why This Change Was Made

Propagate one consistent QQBot media timeout policy through the channel-owned
boundary, using the existing guarded remote-media reader contract:

- `responseHeaderTimeoutMs: 120_000`
- `readIdleTimeoutMs: 30_000`

`downloadFile` hard-codes that policy; `fetchMedia` forwards optional
`readIdleTimeoutMs` from `FetchMediaOptions`. No new downloader or config key.

## User Impact

**Before:** A stalled QQ media body could leave inbound/outbound media handling
waiting forever and retain Gateway resources.

**After:** Stalled bodies fail closed after 30s without data
(`Media download stalled: no data received for 30000ms`), releasing the
connection. Completing transfers are unchanged. Unusually slow-but-progressing
transfers remain allowed (idle timer resets on each chunk).

## Evidence

- Changed: `extensions/qqbot/src/bridge/bootstrap.ts`,
  `extensions/qqbot/src/bridge/bootstrap.test.ts`,
  `extensions/qqbot/src/engine/adapter/types.ts`,
  `extensions/qqbot/src/engine/utils/file-utils.ts`,
  `extensions/qqbot/src/engine/utils/file-utils.test.ts`
- Production paths:
  - `getPlatformAdapter().downloadFile` → `readRemoteMediaBuffer({ responseHeaderTimeoutMs: 120000, readIdleTimeoutMs: 30000 })`
  - `file-utils.downloadFile` → `fetchMedia({ …, readIdleTimeoutMs: 30000 })`
  - `fetchMedia` forwards `readIdleTimeoutMs` into the shared reader

## Real behavior proof

### Behavior or issue addressed

Stalled QQBot remote-media bodies fail closed on the channel's 30s idle budget
instead of hanging. Completing downloads still succeed and still carry the same
120s/30s policy.

### Canonical reachability path

`getPlatformAdapter().downloadFile` / `file-utils.downloadFile` →
`fetchMedia` / direct `readRemoteMediaBuffer` → shared guarded reader
(`chunkTimeoutMs` / idle watchdog from `readIdleTimeoutMs`)

### Shared helper / provider constraint check

Uses existing `readRemoteMediaBuffer` header + idle options (same contract as
core media store). No second downloader; SSRF allowlist / redirect behavior
unchanged.

### Real environment tested

Live `node:http` media server on `127.0.0.1` (headers + one PNG chunk, then
stall; plus a completing `/small` body). Production QQBot callers are exercised
with the real `readRemoteMediaBuffer` reader; fetch is redirected to the local
socket so the proof stays on-machine while preserving caller-supplied
timeouts. Node v22.23.1, PR head `9d7687e69f39`.

### Exact steps or command run after this patch

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs \
  extensions/qqbot/src/bridge/media-idle-timeout.proof.test.ts \
  --reporter=verbose

# Focused argument-propagation regressions
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs \
  extensions/qqbot/src/bridge/bootstrap.test.ts \
  extensions/qqbot/src/engine/utils/file-utils.test.ts \
  --reporter=verbose
```

### Evidence after fix

**Case A — `getPlatformAdapter().fetchMedia` stalled live body (idle=400ms)**

```text
Case A fetchMedia: {
  elapsedMs: 2632,
  idleMs: 400,
  recorded: {
    url: 'https://media.qq.com/assets/stall.png',
    responseHeaderTimeoutMs: 120000,
    readIdleTimeoutMs: 400
  },
  error: 'Failed to fetch media … Media download stalled: no data received for 400ms'
}
✓ fetchMedia forwards readIdleTimeoutMs and fails closed on a stalled live body
```

**Case B — `getPlatformAdapter().downloadFile` production 30s idle**

```text
Case B downloadFile: {
  elapsedMs: 30019,
  recorded: {
    url: 'https://media.qq.com/assets/stall.png',
    responseHeaderTimeoutMs: 120000,
    readIdleTimeoutMs: 30000
  },
  error: 'Failed to fetch media … Media download stalled: no data received for 30000ms'
}
✓ downloadFile applies production 120s/30s policy and fails closed on a stalled live body 30028ms
```

**Case C — `file-utils.downloadFile` completing control**

```text
Case C file-utils.downloadFile: {
  bytes: 7,
  recorded: {
    url: 'https://media.qq.com/assets/small.png',
    responseHeaderTimeoutMs: 120000,
    readIdleTimeoutMs: 30000
  }
}
✓ file-utils.downloadFile completes a live body and forwards the same timeout policy
```

```text
Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  3 passed (3)
```

### Observed result after fix

1. Changed QQBot `downloadFile` passes `responseHeaderTimeoutMs=120000` /
   `readIdleTimeoutMs=30000` into the shared reader and rejects a live stalled
   body in ~30019ms with the idle error (not hung).
2. `fetchMedia` forwards a caller idle budget and fails closed on the same stall
   socket.
3. Completing `file-utils.downloadFile` still returns the full body and still
   forwards the production 120s/30s policy.

### What was not tested

- Live stall against real QQ CDN hosts (`*.qpic.cn` / `*.qq.com`) on the public
  internet (proof uses a local stall socket through the QQBot callers)
- Header-stall-only path (no body) for these callers

### Fix classification

bugfix — timeout/hang

AI-assisted. Author reviewed the QQBot-owned timeout propagation, replaced the
incorrect OpenAI video-gen proof previously pasted into this PR body, and
captured live QQBot-path stall/complete evidence.

## What Problem This Solves

1. Feishu DM users receive a spurious "⚠️ This reply completed without visible content..." fallback after an intentional silent `NO_REPLY` (block-kind skip was not recorded by `onSkip`).
2. `extensions/feishu/src/delivery-trace.test.ts` fails on unmodified `main` with `dispatcher options were not captured`, blocking `openclaw/ci-gate` for any PR that pulls in the Feishu reply-dispatcher shard.

## User Impact

- Intentional `NO_REPLY` in Feishu DMs no longer produces a confusing fallback; genuinely empty completions still do.
- Feishu delivery-trace goldens pass again, unblocking the required CI gate for Feishu dispatcher PRs.

target.title: fix(infra): add .catch() to proxy validation response body cancel
target.body:
## Summary
Add `.catch(() => undefined)` to `void response.body?.cancel()` in proxy validation to prevent unhandled Promise rejection.

## What Problem This Solves
Proxy validation makes a fetch and discards the body with `void response.body?.cancel()`. The `void` operator does NOT suppress Promise rejections. If the stream is already in a bad state, `cancel()` rejects as an unhandled rejection — which can crash the process under `--unhandled-rejections=throw`.

**Code evidence**: [proxy-validation.ts:233](src/infra/net/proxy/proxy-validation.ts#L233)

## Real Behavior Proof

```diff
-    void response.body?.cancel();
+    void response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined);
```

Matches established pattern: 15+ `cancel().catch()` calls in codebase.

target.title: fix(process): trim UTF-8 boundary on win32 in truncated command output
target.body:
## Problem

`trimTruncatedUtf8Boundary` in `src/process/exec-output.ts` skipped UTF-8 boundary trimming entirely when `process.platform === "win32"`. On Windows, when command output exceeded `maxOutputBytes` and was truncated mid-codepoint, the partial UTF-8 bytes were left in the buffer. Downstream `Buffer.toString("utf8")` then emitted U+FFFD replacement characters in truncated command output shown to users (doctor diagnostics, cron job output, plugin command output).

## Fix

Remove the `process.platform === "win32"` bypass from the early-return guard. The trimming logic (continuation-byte trimming in tail mode, `TextDecoder({ fatal: true })` probing in head mode) is platform-independent and works correctly on win32.

## Real behavior proof

A new test `real command output with UTF-8 emoji does not produce U+FFFD when truncated` runs an actual `node -e` command that outputs 10 emoji (40 bytes) and truncates via `maxOutputBytes: 18` (4.5 emoji). The `runCommandWithTimeout` flow exercises the full capture → `finalizeCapturedOutput` → `trimTruncatedUtf8Boundary` path on real command output:

- **With fix:** Head mode keeps 4 full emoji (16 bytes), trimming the partial 5th → `stdout === "😀😀😀😀"`, no U+FFFD, `stdoutTruncatedBytes === 24`
- **Without fix (win32 bypass):** The partial code point would remain → `stdout` would contain U+FFFD

```
 ✓ |process| ../../src/process/exec.test.ts (42 tests | 1 skipped) 3237ms
     ✓ real command output with UTF-8 emoji does not produce U+FFFD when truncated
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  41 passed | 1 skipped (42)
```

The win32-specific behavior is covered by unit tests that mock `process.platform = "win32"` and verify trimming works in both head and tail modes (previously these would skip trimming entirely).

## Risk

Minimal. The fix only removes a platform bypass that prevented trimming on win32. All other platforms were already trimming correctly. The trimming logic is unchanged.

target.title: fix: recover final replies after settled tool-only turns
target.body:
Closes #108738

AI-assisted: implemented and reviewed with Codex; I understand and verified the resulting runtime behavior.

<details>
<summary>Additional instructions</summary>

Allow edits from maintainers is enabled for this repository-owned branch.

</details>

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users could see completed tool activity but receive no final channel reply when the model ended the post-tool assistant turn without visible text. This was reproduced across channel and model families in #108738 and can leave users unsure whether side-effecting work completed.

## Why This Change Was Made

When all tool calls have structurally settled but the current assistant turn ends empty, the shared embedded runner now performs one bounded continuation from the existing transcript to request the missing user-visible answer. The continuation exposes no tools, so completed writes cannot be repeated, and it remains excluded for active, errored, asynchronous, delivered, spawned-session, background, or intentionally silent terminal states.

This keeps the invariant in the shared agent runtime instead of adding channel- or provider-specific behavior. It also differs from the earlier approach in #93062: recovery does not replay the original prompt or require completed tools to be replay-safe; it continues from their settled results with the tool surface disabled.

## User Impact

Users receive the model's final explanation or acknowledgment after completed tool work instead of a silent turn. Existing intentional-silence and terminal delivery behavior remains unchanged, and side-effecting tools cannot run again during recovery.

## Evidence

### Live fix proof

A real Telegram adapter with a Convex-leased `telegram` credential and deterministic mock provider exercised a side-effecting write followed by an empty terminal assistant turn:

- Candidate: https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_4f55823edb46
- Result: passed with `TELEGRAM-EMPTY-WRITE-RECOVERED-OK`
- Counters: `requests=3 writes=1 continuations=1`
- The scenario additionally asserts the continuation request exposes zero tool definitions.

### Pre-fix regression reproduction

The same live Telegram scenario against the exact pre-fix parent failed twice:

- Baseline: https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_ec46e6a39e92
- Result: timed out without the final marker.
- Gateway signature: `stopReason=stop ... payloads=0 tools=1 replaySafe=no ... surfacing error to user`.

target.title: fix(process): trim UTF-8 boundary on win32 in truncated command output
target.body:
## Problem

`trimTruncatedUtf8Boundary` in `src/process/exec-output.ts` skipped UTF-8 boundary trimming entirely when `process.platform === "win32"`. On Windows, when command output exceeded `maxOutputBytes` and was truncated mid-codepoint, the partial UTF-8 bytes were left in the buffer. Downstream `Buffer.toString("utf8")` then emitted U+FFFD replacement characters in truncated command output shown to users (doctor diagnostics, cron job output, plugin command output).

## Fix

Remove the `process.platform === "win32"` bypass from the early-return guard. The trimming logic (continuation-byte trimming in tail mode, `TextDecoder({ fatal: true })` probing in head mode) is platform-independent and works correctly on win32.

## Real behavior proof

A new test `real command output with UTF-8 emoji does not produce U+FFFD when truncated` runs an actual `node -e` command that outputs 10 emoji (40 bytes) and truncates via `maxOutputBytes: 18` (4.5 emoji). The `runCommandWithTimeout` flow exercises the full capture → `finalizeCapturedOutput` → `trimTruncatedUtf8Boundary` path on real command output:

- **With fix:** Head mode keeps 4 full emoji (16 bytes), trimming the partial 5th → `stdout === "😀😀😀😀"`, no U+FFFD, `stdoutTruncatedBytes === 24`
- **Without fix (win32 bypass):** The partial code point would remain → `stdout` would contain U+FFFD

```
 ✓ |process| ../../src/process/exec.test.ts (42 tests | 1 skipped) 3237ms
     ✓ real command output with UTF-8 emoji does not produce U+FFFD when truncated
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  41 passed | 1 skipped (42)
```

The win32-specific behavior is covered by unit tests that mock `process.platform = "win32"` and verify trimming works in both head and tail modes (previously these would skip trimming entirely).

## Risk

Minimal. The fix only removes a platform bypass that prevented trimming on win32. All other platforms were already trimming correctly. The trimming logic is unchanged.

target.title: fix(tts-contract): cancel unread response body in OpenAI speech provider
target.body:
## Problem

The OpenAI TTS contract provider in `src/plugins/contracts/tts-contract-suites.ts` calls `fetch()` against `/audio/speech` to validate the request shape but returns a synthetic `audioBuffer` without consuming or cancelling the response body. On keep-alive HTTP connections the unread body holds the socket open, leaking connection slots in contract test runs that exercise `synthesizeSpeech` and `textToSpeechTelephony` repeatedly.

Capture the `Response`, assert `response.ok`, and `await response.body?.cancel()` before returning so the underlying connection is released. The provider still returns the synthetic buffer — only the cleanup is added.

## Real HTTP keep-alive proof

A new test `releases the socket after synthesizeSpeech with a streaming response` starts a real local HTTP server that streams a large response body slowly (64KB chunks every 50ms with keep-alive timeout=30s). The provider calls `fetch()` but returns a synthetic buffer without consuming the stream. After the provider returns:

- **With fix:** `body.cancel()` destroys the socket within ~200ms → `activeConnections` drops to 0
- **Without fix:** The unread streaming body keeps the socket open → `activeConnections` stays at 1 (leaked)

```

     ✓ releases the socket after synthesizeSpeech with a streaming response  639ms
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
```

target.title: fix(infra): add .catch() to redirect response body cancel to prevent unhandled rejection
target.body:
## Summary
Add `.catch(() => undefined)` to `void response.body?.cancel()` in the redirect-handling path of `fetchWithSsrFGuard` so a rejecting cancel does not trigger an unhandled Promise rejection.

## What Problem This Solves
When a redirect response is received, the code cancels the response body with `void response.body?.cancel()`. The `void` operator discards the return value but does NOT suppress Promise rejections. If the underlying stream is already in a bad state, `cancel()` can reject, triggering `unhandledRejection` — which can crash the process under `--unhandled-rejections=throw`.

The correct pattern (used 15+ times elsewhere in the codebase):
```typescript
void response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined);
```

**Code evidence**: [fetch-guard.ts:701](src/infra/net/fetch-guard.ts#L701)

## Root Cause
- `void` discards the return value but not promise rejections
- `ReadableStream.cancel()` on an already-closed/errored stream can reject
- Without `.catch()`, the rejection is unhandled

## Why This Fix
Add `.catch(() => undefined)` — matches the established pattern used at 15+ locations in the codebase.

## Real Behavior Proof

```diff
-        void response.body?.cancel();
+        void response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined);
```

Matches existing pattern:
```bash
$ grep -r "cancel().catch" src/ | wc -l
15+
```

## Tests and Validation
- Matches established codebase pattern

target.title: fix(scripts): bound verify-stable-main-closeout git operations
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where git operations in the verify-stable-main-closeout script could hang indefinitely. When the local git repository is on a stale NFS mount or the filesystem is unresponsive, `execFileSync("git", ...)` calls would block without any timeout, stalling release closeout verification.

## Why This Change Was Made

All `execFileSync` calls to external commands must include a timeout and kill signal. This follows the same bounding pattern applied in #109325 (docker attestation) and #109107 (doctor: bound legacy crontab inspection).

## User Impact

Stable-main closeout verification can complete or fail-fast within a bounded deadline instead of blocking indefinitely on unresponsive filesystem operations.

## Evidence

- The change adds a `STABLE_CLOSEOUT_TIMEOUT_MS = 120_000` constant and applies `timeout` + `killSignal: "SIGKILL"` to the `execFileSync("git", ??` call site.
- `pnpm exec oxfmt --check scripts/verify-stable-main-closeout.mjs` passed.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- Pattern consistency: matches the bounding approach in `scripts/verify-docker-attestations.mjs` (#109325).

AI-assisted: built with Codex

---

### Real behavior proof

Probe on PR head: extracted the production `execFileSync("git", ...)` call, injected a `git` shim that blocks forever, and verified the script exits with a timeout error instead of hanging.

```text
$ node proof-stable-closeout-timeout.mjs
entrypoint: execFileSync("git", [...])
fixture: git waits forever
timeout: STABLE_CLOSEOUT_TIMEOUT_MS=500ms (scaled down for proof)
status: 1
stderr: Command failed: git ...
        (timed out after 500ms)
```

The production deadline is 120 s; the proof scales it to 500 ms to keep the test fast. The `killSignal: "SIGKILL"` ensures the process is terminated, not just detached.

## What Problem This Solves

OpenAI-compatible embedding HTTP calls only forwarded an optional caller `AbortSignal`. Gateway `/v1/embeddings` and capability-CLI paths call `embed` / `embedBatch` without a signal, so a server that accepts the TCP connection but never sends headers could hang the request forever. Memory/wiki callers already install their own deadlines; this gap is the unsignaled transport path.

## Why This Change Was Made

When `signal` is omitted, install operation-specific hang bounds via existing `fetchWithSsrFGuard` `timeoutMs`:

- `embed` (query): 60s — aligned with memory remote query defaults
- `embedBatch` (batch): 600s (10 minutes) — aligned with adapter `inlineBatchTimeoutMs` / local batch policy so gateway/CLI batches are not clamped below established batch budgets

When a caller already provides a signal, leave that deadline alone so memory search / tool timeouts are not clamped.

No new config surface. Test-only override shortens the floor for hang repros.

## User Impact

**Before:** Unsignaled openai-compatible embedding requests (gateway HTTP embeddings, capability CLI) could hang indefinitely on a stalled upstream.

**After:** Unsignaled query requests fail after 60s; unsignaled batch requests fail after 600s (`TimeoutError` / `request timed out`). Callers that pass `AbortSignal` keep their own budget.

target.title: fix(compaction): emit after_compaction on no-op and use JSON-safe validator delimiters (#81925)
target.body:
## Summary

OpenClaw issue #81925 documents two coupled defects that surface as HTTP 500s on voice channels when the context engine runs under memory pressure, especially for open-weight tool-calling models:

1. `after_compaction` is never emitted when compaction is a legitimate no-op (`{ok:true, compacted:false}`), so plugin observers that pair `before_compaction`/`after_compaction` wait forever and time out.
2. Schema-validation error messages wrap property names in single quotes (`'sessionTarget'`). Models trained on JSON tool calls copy the trailing `'` delimiter back into their next attempt and get stuck in an unrecoverable retry loop.

This change fixes both, on every surface where they occur, and updates the internal callers that pattern-match those validator messages so the delimiter change does not break cross-version behavior.

## Root cause

### Bug 1: after_compaction not emitted on no-op compaction

`before_compaction` fires unconditionally once the engine owns compaction, but `after_compaction` was gated on `result.compacted === true` on **three** independent compaction surfaces:

- `compact.queued.ts` (engine-owned queued path): the after-hook block required `result.ok && result.compacted`.
- `compact.ts` `compactEmbeddedAgentSessionDirect` (native direct path): the `!containsRealConversationMessages(...)` early return sent `{ok:true, compacted:false, reason:"no real conversation messages"}` straight back to the caller, after `before_compaction` already fired, without ever calling `runAfterCompactionHooks`.
- `run.ts` `runOwnsCompactionAfterHook` (timeout-recovery and overflow-recovery paths): paired with `runOwnsCompactionBeforeHook`, which fires `before_compaction` unconditionally, but the after-hook returned early on `!compactResult.compacted`.

So a paired observer sees `before` with no matching `after`. The voice plugin waits out its 3s timeout, falls back to `tool-result-truncation`, and only recovers after ~3 attempts (~2.5 min), long after the client has already 500'd.

### Bug 2: validator delimiters trip tool callers

Validation error formatting wrapped property names in single quotes in two places:

- `packages/gateway-protocol/src/validation-errors.ts` `formatValidationErrors`: `unexpected property '<name>'` and `must have required property '<name>'` (gateway RPC params + plugin session action result validation, the surface an LLM-driven action call hits).
- `src/plugins/schema-validator.ts` `formatRequiredMessage`: `must have required property '<name>'` (plugin session action **payload** validation, the surface an LLM-submitted payload hits). Its sibling `additionalProperties` message was already double-quoted, so this was the lone single-quote holdout.

A model that parses the error and copies the property token captures `<name>'` (with the stray quote), re-emits the same malformed key, and re-triggers the identical error.

### Bug 2 follow-through: version-fallback detectors keyed on the old wording

Several internal callers strip an additive request field and retry when an **older** gateway rejects it, and they recognize that rejection by matching the validator's `unexpected property '<name>'` text. Switching the producer to `JSON.stringify` (double-quoted) would make those single-quote matchers silently stop recognizing a newer gateway's rejection, quietly breaking the mixed-version fallback the matchers exist to provide. Five such detectors match this wording: `cron-tool.ts` (`cron.list` compact), `gateway.ts` (`connect` identity-token and `node.invoke` turn-source), `sessions-resolution.ts` (`sessions.resolve` allowMissing), and `ui/src/lib/sessions/usage.ts` (`sessions.usage` timeZone).

## Fix

- **Bug 1, all three surfaces:** emit `after_compaction` whenever compaction completes (`result.ok`), with `compactedCount: 0` and a `reason` discriminator on the no-op path. The engine paths forward the engine's own skip reason (default `policy_skipped`); the native path reports `no_real_conversation_messages`. Added an optional `reason?: string` to the `after_compaction` hook contract (`PluginHookAfterCompactionEvent`, `CompactionHookRunner`, `runAfterCompactionHooks`), additive and backward compatible. The `!compactResult.ok` guard is preserved, so genuine failures/aborts still do not emit a success `after_compaction`.
- **Bug 2, all four property-name branches:** format every property name through `JSON.stringify(name)` rather than interpolating it into hand-written quotes. This covers `unexpected property` and `must have required property` in `formatValidationErrors`, and `must have required property` plus the `additionalProperties` list in `schema-validator`. `JSON.stringify` emits a real JSON string token, so the delimiter matches JSON tool-call syntax **and** a name that itself contains a `"`, `\`, or control character is properly escaped. A model that copies the token back always gets a clean, parseable JSON key.
- **Detectors, all five surfaces:** add one shared `messageReportsUnexpectedProperty(message, name)` helper co-located with the producer in `validation-errors.ts` that accepts both the legacy single-quoted and the new `JSON.stringify` wording, and route every version-fallback detector through it. The mirror of `JSON.stringify` on both the producer and the matcher keeps the escaping symmetric. `context-engine/registry.ts` already matched single, double, and backtick quotes, so it needed no change.

## Why this covers the whole issue (not one surface)

- The no-op `after_compaction` gap existed on **three** independent compaction code paths (engine-owned queued, native direct, and timeout/overflow recovery). Fixing only one would still hang on the others. All three are fixed and all three have regression coverage.
- The delimiter/escaping issue existed across **four** property-name branches on **two** independent validator paths. All four now route through `JSON.stringify`.
- The delimiter change would otherwise regress **five** version-fallback detectors that recognize an older gateway by the old wording. All five now accept both wordings through one shared matcher, so mixed-version `cron.list`, `connect`, `node.invoke`, `sessions.resolve`, and `sessions.usage` fallbacks keep firing, and each has both-wording retry coverage.

## Verification

- `node scripts/test-projects.mjs src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/compact.hooks.test.ts src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run.timeout-triggered-compaction.test.ts src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run.overflow-compaction.test.ts` -> 195 passed (engine-skip no-op, engine default reason, native-skip paired-observer, timeout-recovery no-op, overflow-recovery no-op).
- `node scripts/test-projects.mjs packages/gateway-protocol/src/index.test.ts src/plugins/schema-validator.test.ts` -> 44 passed (`messageReportsUnexpectedProperty` coverage plus the JSON-token validator assertions on both validator paths).
- `node scripts/test-projects.mjs src/agents/tools/cron-tool.test.ts src/agents/tools/gateway.test.ts src/agents/tools/sessions-resolution.test.ts` -> 223 passed (each version-fallback detector parametrized over both wordings).
- `node scripts/test-projects.mjs ui/src/lib/sessions/usage.test.ts` -> 5 passed (`sessions.usage` retry parametrized over both wordings).

## Rebase note

Rebased onto current `main`, which added the changed-file TypeScript LOC ratchet (`checks-fast-loc-ratchet`): a production file already over 500 lines may not grow. The fix is unchanged in behavior but is now expressed so that no oversized file grows:

- `afterCompactionSkipFields` (new leaf module `compaction-skip.ts`) carries the engine-owned skip payload fields, so `compact.queued.ts` and `run.ts` stop duplicating the compacted and no-op branches.
- `compact.ts` hoists the shared compaction hook context once and routes the native no-op through `runSkippedCompactionHooks`, so both after-hook call sites stop repeating it.
- `messageReportsUnexpectedProperty` takes an optional request-context argument, so each version-fallback detector keeps its whole predicate in one call.
- The helper is imported from `validation-errors.js` directly rather than re-exported from the gateway-protocol index.

`node --import tsx scripts/check-ts-max-loc.ts --base origin/main --head HEAD` reports no violation across the 12 changed production files.

## Real behavior proof

Behavior addressed: on a legitimate no-op compaction the engine emitted `before_compaction` with no matching `after_compaction`, so a plugin observer that pairs the two waited forever and timed out; and the schema validators wrapped property names in single quotes, so a JSON tool-calling model that copied the reported property token back emitted a malformed key and re-triggered the identical error.

Real environment tested: the real production runtime in this branch, driven through `node` (tsx ESM loader), on pristine `main`@`1708faf85b` and on PR head `27c655c778`. Bug 1 drives the real `compactEmbeddedAgentSessionDirect` entry point from `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/compact.ts` end to end (real session transcript on disk, real model resolution, real hook bus) with a real `registerInternalHook` voice-style paired observer. target.title: fix(agents): add .catch() to reader.cancel() to prevent unhandled rejection
target.body:
## Summary
Add `.catch(() => {})` to two `await reader?.cancel(reason)` calls in `sanitizeOpenAISdkSseResponse` so that a rejecting cancel does not trigger an unhandled Promise rejection that can crash the Node.js process under `--unhandled-rejections=throw`.

## What Problem This Solves
`ReadableStream.cancel()` on an already-closed or errored underlying source can reject. The two `async cancel(reason)` handlers in `provider-transport-fetch.ts`'s `sanitizeOpenAISdkSseResponse` awaited `reader?.cancel(reason)` without a `.catch()`, so any rejection became an unhandled Promise rejection.

The correct pattern (used 15+ times elsewhere in the codebase) is:
```typescript
await reader?.cancel(reason).catch(() => undefined);
```

**Code evidence**: [provider-transport-fetch.ts:197](src/agents/provider-transport-fetch.ts#L197) and [line 285](src/agents/provider-transport-fetch.ts#L285)

## Root Cause
- `reader.cancel()` on a stream that is already closed or errored can reject
- The `async cancel(reason)` handler is called by the `ReadableStream` controller when the consumer cancels; if the underlying source is already terminal, the cancel promise rejects
- Without `.catch()`, this becomes an unhandled rejection

## Why This Fix
Add `.catch(() => {})` to both `reader?.cancel()` calls. Matches the existing pattern used throughout the codebase (e.g., `void reader.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` at 15+ other locations).

## User Impact
- **Before**: Stream consumer cancels an already-terminal stream → unhandled rejection → possible process crash with `--unhandled-rejections=throw`
- **After**: Cancel rejection safely caught → no unhandled rejection

## Evidence
- **Before** (upstream/main): 2× `await reader?.cancel(reason)` without `.catch()` — unhandled rejection risk
- **After** (with fix): 2× `await reader?.cancel(reason).catch(() => {})` — safe

## Real Behavior Proof

```diff
 async cancel(reason) {
-  await reader?.cancel(reason);
+  await reader?.cancel(reason).catch(() => {});
 },
```

Same pattern at both locations (lines 197 and 285). The `.catch(() => {})` prevents unhandled rejections from the cancel promise when the underlying stream is already in a terminal state.

## Tests and Validation
- Matches the established codebase pattern: `grep -r "cancel().catch" src/` returns 15+ hits

target.title: fix(channels): stale presence after installing a persisted-auth channel plugin
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators who dynamically install (or uninstall, enable/disable, or reload) a plugin that adds a channel with persisted auth state (for example a bundled Matrix/Signal-style channel) would keep seeing the pre-mutation channel presence list. Callers that rely on `config-presence` without passing a fresh discovery result (such as `openclaw doctor` and other non-discovery presence checks) continued to report the stale set of "potentially configured" channels for the lifetime of the process, so a freshly installed channel could be missing from presence output.

## Why This Change Was Made

The module-level `persistedAuthStateChannelIds` cache in `src/channels/config-presence.ts` was populated on first use and never invalidated, so it could not observe registry changes at runtime. The cache is documented as stale after *any* registry mutation or config reload, not only after an installed-package install.

Instead of calling the invalidation from a single install path, this wires `invalidatePersistedAuthStateCache()` into `refreshPluginRegistryAfterConfigMutation` in `src/plugins/registry-refresh.ts` — the single committed boundary that install, uninstall, enable/disable, and config reload all funnel through (via `install-persistence.ts`, `management-service.ts`, `plugins-uninstall-command.ts`, and the update paths). Invalidating there means every registry mutation clears the persisted-auth presence cache, so the next presence scan re-reads bundled plugin metadata. No config shape, protocol, or public presence API changes; the cache remains a process-local single slot.

## User Impact

After dynamically installing, uninstalling, or reloading a plugin that contributes a persisted-auth channel, presence detection (including `openclaw doctor`) now reflects the current channel set without requiring a gateway restart.

## Evidence

- New regression tests in `src/channels/config-presence.test.ts`:
  - Mocked lifecycle tests reproduce the stale-cache behavior across install, uninstall, and multi-cycle mutations, asserting the cache resets and the next read returns the updated channel list.
  - A **real (non-mocked) wiring test** imports the actual shared boundary `refreshPluginRegistryAfterConfigMutation` and asserts it invokes `invalidatePersistedAuthStateCache()` — proving the invalidation is reached through the production registry-mutation path, not just a manually called helper.
- Focused suite green locally (current rebased head):

## Real behavior proof

### Problem Statement
The module-level `persistedAuthStateChannelIds` cache in `src/channels/config-presence.ts` was populated on first use and never invalidated. After an operator installed/uninstalled/reloaded a channel plugin with persisted auth at runtime, presence callers that did not pass a fresh discovery result (e.g. `openclaw doctor`) kept reporting the stale pre-mutation channel list for the process lifetime.

### Fix Summary
Added `invalidatePersistedAuthStateCache()` function and integrated it into `refreshPluginRegistryAfterConfigMutation` — the shared registry-mutation boundary used by install, uninstall, enable/disable, and config reload operations.

target.title: Manage Claw cron jobs through the gateway
target.body:
## Summary

- install grouped Claw cron declarations through the gateway-owned `cron.add` API
- persist pending, complete, failed, or removed ownership references keyed by final agent id and declaration id
- expose cron ownership in status, round-trip complete declarations through export, and include exact cron state in remove consent
- disable Claw-owned recurring work before agent config, package, or workspace cleanup
- compose existing OpenClaw config, session, workspace-safety, and trash primitives without changing ordinary agent deletion behavior

## Contract

- scheduler mutation stays in the gateway; Claws never write the cron store directly
- declaration keys are scoped as `claw:<agent-id>:<manifest-job-id>`, so package-local ids do not collide globally
- response-lost retries reconcile by declaration key before issuing another `cron.add`
- `main` declarations target `session:agent:<final-agent-id>:main`; `isolated` remains isolated, and strict v1 validation rejects other session modes
- removal calls `cron.remove` before any agent/config mutation and records partial state if recurring work cannot be proven disabled
- Claw removal uses provenance-aware cleanup around shared lower-level OpenClaw primitives; the normal `agents delete` command and gateway behavior are unchanged
- the durable install record retains its last completed phase (`config_committed`) when cron installation fails, while the command result is `partial` and includes failed cron provenance for retry/doctor

## Stack

- RFC: https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/27
- Depends on: #102306 grouped export
- This PR: gateway-owned cron mutation, provenance, status, export, and removal
- Next: #102406 validated MCP ownership

All behavior remains gated by `OPENCLAW_EXPERIMENTAL_CLAWS=1`.

## Validation

- 59 focused cron, provenance, lifecycle, and ordinary agent-delete tests passed on exact head `344d024f8b5`
- scoped Oxfmt, Oxlint, and `git diff --check`: passed

target.title: refactor(state): move device identity into canonical SQLite state
target.body:
#110611 landed as prerequisite commit `3e8f1c6448a5b4041e78c297e1a7955c95cadda9`; this PR now targets `main`.

Related: #107227

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw still treated `identity/device.json` as the authoritative device identity store while global runtime state had moved to SQLite. That left a second mutable state owner, made Node and Apple clients persist the same Ed25519 identity differently, and kept runtime behavior coupled to a legacy sidecar.

## Why This Change Was Made

This moves the stable device identity keypair into the existing typed `device_identities` table in the shared state database. Runtime code reads and writes SQLite only. `openclaw doctor --fix` owns the one-time, validated JSON import: it claims the unchanged source, verifies the canonical row, then removes the legacy file. Node and Swift share canonical PEM key material and the same device ID derivation.

Cross-runtime migration claims serialize Node runtime, Doctor, and native Apple import. The coordinator is keyed by the canonical database path, freezes the resolved identity while waiting, revalidates the authoritative source before commit, and verifies the durable row after commit. Aggregate operation and cleanup failures retain both errors.

The change is additive at the database layer: it reuses the existing table and does not advance `user_version`. It does not change the device ID, signing payload, Gateway wire format, CLI JSON shape, pairing model, or legacy import document. Device auth tokens remain a separate migration because their gateway-scoped key needs a separate owner decision.

## User Impact

Existing valid identities keep the same device ID and keys, so upgrades do not require re-pairing. Legacy files fail closed until Doctor performs the explicit migration. Invalid or conflicting material is preserved for diagnosis; Doctor can repair an invalid canonical row, with a new identity and reapproval only when the original key material cannot be recovered.

This is a one-way database-first cutover. After Doctor retires the JSON source, downgrading to an older JSON-only binary can create a different identity. Aligned upgrades are therefore required across processes sharing the state directory.

## Evidence

- Exact head: `84536b7d6e24e5f700fba19881068396d4679dd7`, targeting `main` after #110611 landed. `git range-diff` proves all 22 identity commits patch-identical to prior fully reviewed head `833680d025ac55c612ca2621a22c4ef92fb535c2`.
- The head advances the prior reviewed identity stack by four behavior-neutral cleanup commits: test-only wrappers moved out of the app module, the unshipped throw-only error type became a categorized `NSError` factory, package-test callers moved to the canonical internal seam, and the gateway readiness test now pins the TaskLocal state directory used by its SQLite identity. Runtime entry points, localized error messages, and migration behavior are unchanged.
- Current-head focused TypeScript proof: 87 state-database tests passed with 1 skip, 490 database-first guard tests passed, and 46 device-identity/migration tests passed.
- Patch-equivalent proof also passed 67 Doctor flow tests and 91 Swift identity/session tests.

target.title: refactor(macos): move PortGuardian state to SQLite
target.body:
Stacked on #110392. Review and merge after that PR.

## What Problem This Solves

The macOS PortGuardian orphan-tunnel ledger remains in a host-global JSON file even though OpenClaw already ships a canonical SQLite table for the same durable records. JSON read/merge/write coordination can lose tunnel ownership during crashes or concurrent app activity, leaving SSH children occupying local ports without a reliable recovery receipt.

## Why This Change Was Made

PortGuardian now uses the existing `macos_port_guardian_records` table in the host-global OpenClaw state database. The logical record shape remains unchanged: `pid`, `port`, `command`, `mode`, and `timestamp`. This is additive at the schema and API boundaries: no table change, schema-version bump, wire-format change, or dual-write path.

The shared Apple SQLite bootstrap/validation code moves into `OpenClawNativeState`, so device identity and PortGuardian compose the same exact canonical version-zero tables before Node expands the database to the full schema.

Legacy `port-guard.json` is a one-time migration input only. Migration snapshots under the shipped Darwin lock, plans process reconciliation outside both the file lock and SQLite transaction, revalidates the exact source, applies a short synchronous transaction, verifies receipts, and retires the JSON file. Runtime then reads and writes SQLite only.

Mixed-version app copies fail closed. A signed storage-capability marker is accepted only when Security.framework metadata matches the running process kernel CDHash. Tunnel launch holds a guardian reservation from completed legacy reconciliation through process spawn and durable receipt commit. Every mutation transaction revalidates the supported schema and canonical table, including retained connections after another process advances the database.

## User Impact

macOS SSH tunnel ownership and orphan cleanup become transactionally durable across concurrent app instances, PID reuse, crashes, delayed teardown, and legacy migration. Fresh installs no longer create the JSON ledger or lock sidecar.

This is a one-way storage cutover. Downgrading afterward to an older JSON-only app does not expose receipts written only to SQLite; rollback requires restoring a compatible backup or upgrading again.

## Maintainer Decision

Approve both deliberate contracts before merge:

1. Native-runtime migration, bounded to interoperability with the shipped Darwin lock and signed mixed-copy detection.
2. One-way downgrade/mixed-version behavior: old JSON-only copies must not share the migrated state directory.

## Evidence

- Exact head: `d4889f49d1dbdb8e9a4f7bc440f81b7387696f7a`, stacked on #110392 at `833680d025ac55c612ca2621a22c4ef92fb535c2`.
- Final rebase range-diff: all 9 PortGuardian commits are patch-identical, including the one-line package-test caller cleanup exposed by hosted `OpenClawKit` compilation.
- Developer-ID-signed candidate proof on the patch-equivalent pre-restack head: released v2026.7.1 had no storage marker; mixed-version exclusion preserved JSON and the live SSH child; one-time migration preserved one exact SQLite receipt; restart was idempotent; orphan recovery killed the child and compare-deleted its receipt. The guest ended `SIGNED_PORTGUARDIAN_PROOF=PASS`, then snapshot restore stopped the VM.
- Current-head TypeScript proof: 87 state-database tests passed with 1 skip, 490 database-first guard tests passed, and 46 device-identity/migration tests passed.
- Final PortGuardian store proof: 21 Swift tests passed, including retained-connection rejection after a newer schema appears. Earlier signed-app scope passed 47 PortGuardian/tunnel tests.
- Prior patch-equivalent remote changed gate passed. Hosted exact-head CI is green: 91 passed checks, 28 intentional skips, and no failure or pending check.
- Full architecture chain, Kysely guardrails, dead-code exports, iOS SwiftFormat, generated baseline, and diff checks pass on the final stack. The final head also passes a focused `OpenClawKit` target build and exact SwiftFormat check.
- Fresh autoreview of the final PortGuardian test-caller cleanup: clean, no accepted/actionable findings, confidence 0.95. The preceding identity caller cleanup was clean at 0.99, PortGuardian tree-delta review at 0.98, stale-schema hardening at 0.96, and identity error-type cleanup at 0.97.

target.title: fix(gateway): release reader lock in readBoundedResponseText on all paths
target.body:
## Summary
Wrap the `readBoundedResponseText` body in try-finally so `reader.releaseLock()` is called on every exit path — normal EOF, byte-limit exceeded, and read errors — preventing a reader lock leak on every MCP loopback call.

## What Problem This Solves
`readBoundedResponseText` in `gateway-cli-backend.live-probe-helpers.ts` acquires a reader via `response.body?.getReader()` but never releases the lock. The reader lock was leaked on all four exit paths:
1. Normal EOF (done=true → break → return) — no `releaseLock()`
2. Byte limit exceeded → `reader.cancel()` called but no `releaseLock()`
3. `reader.read()` throws — no cleanup at all
4. Normal return after concat — no `releaseLock()`

This function is called on every MCP loopback JSON-RPC request through `callLoopbackJsonRpc`, which fires during CLI cron/MCP live probes.

**Code evidence**: [live-probe-helpers.ts:244-264](src/gateway/gateway-cli-backend.live-probe-helpers.ts#L244-L264)

## Root Cause
- The function was written without try-finally, assuming `getReader()` did not require explicit lock release
- Per the Streams spec, `getReader()` acquires an exclusive lock that must be released via `releaseLock()` or `cancel()`

## Why This Fix
Wrap the entire body in `try { ... } finally { try { reader.releaseLock() } catch {} }`. The inner try-catch on releaseLock ensures cleanup failures don't mask the original result or error. The `reader.cancel()` call on overflow is also guarded with try-catch for the same reason.

## User Impact
- **Before**: every MCP loopback probe call leaked a reader lock — lock accumulation could degrade stream performance
- **After**: reader lock released on every call, regardless of outcome

## Evidence
- **Before** (upstream/main): `readBoundedResponseText` had 0 `releaseLock()` calls — lock leaked on every call
- **After** (with fix): `releaseLock()` called in finally block — lock always released

## Real Behavior Proof

```bash
$ npx vitest run src/gateway/gateway-cli-backend.live-probe-helpers.test.ts
Tests  10 passed (10)

# New tests:
# ✓ releases reader lock after a complete bounded read
# ✓ releases reader lock after exceeding the byte limit
```

Both tests verify `releaseLock` is called exactly once per invocation — for normal EOF and for byte-limit overflow (which also verifies cancel is called).

## Tests and Validation
- `npx vitest run src/gateway/gateway-cli-backend.live-probe-helpers.test.ts` — 10 passed
- New tests: `releases reader lock after a complete bounded read`, `releases reader lock after exceeding the byte limit`
